question: What is the difference between REST and SOAP?
title: REST vs SOAP
direct_answer: REST is an architectural style using HTTP with JSON/XML, emphasizing simplicity and statelessness. SOAP is a protocol with strict XML-based messaging, built-in error handling (WSDL/SOAP faults), and enterprise features like WS-Security. REST dominates modern web APIs; SOAP persists in enterprise/banking systems.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of different API paradigms and ability to choose the right one
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying SOAP is just old REST or not knowing when SOAP is still appropriate
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that SOAP has advantages in transaction management, security, and ACID compliance

sections.title: REST vs SOAP Comparison
sections.content: REST and SOAP are both ways to build APIs but with fundamentally different philosophies. REST is lightweight and flexible — use any HTTP method, any data format, no predefined contract required. SOAP is heavyweight and strict — XML only, WSDL contract required, built-in standards for security, transactions, and reliability.

sections.title: Key Differences
content: REST: architectural style; SOAP: protocol with specs
REST: JSON or XML; SOAP: XML only
REST: uses HTTP methods (GET, POST, etc.); SOAP: only POST
REST: no formal contract; SOAP: WSDL file defines contract
REST: stateless; SOAP: can maintain state
SOAP advantages: WS-Security, WS-ReliableMessaging, ACID transactions
REST dominates: APIs, mobile backends, microservices
SOAP still used: banking (SWIFT), government services, legacy enterprise

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: REST is an architectural style — flexible, uses HTTP verbs, typically JSON, no formal contract needed. SOAP is a full protocol — everything is XML, uses only POST, and requires a WSDL contract file that describes every operation. For most modern web and mobile APIs, REST is the right choice — it's simpler and faster to develop. SOAP still makes sense in industries with strict compliance needs like banking and healthcare, because it has built-in standards for security, reliable messaging, and transactions that aren't native to REST.

followup_questions: When would you choose SOAP over REST today?

question: What is GraphQL and how does it compare to REST?
title: GraphQL vs REST
direct_answer: GraphQL is a query language for APIs where clients specify exactly what data they need. Unlike REST (multiple endpoints, fixed response shape), GraphQL has one endpoint and returns exactly what's requested — no over-fetching or under-fetching.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of modern API alternatives and their tradeoffs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying GraphQL is always better — it has real downsides (complexity, caching difficulty)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention N+1 problem in GraphQL and data loader pattern

sections.title: GraphQL Core Concept
sections.content: In REST, you GET /users/1 and get all user fields whether you need them or not. Then GET /users/1/posts for posts. GraphQL lets you send one query: { user(id: 1) { name, posts { title } } } and get exactly that structure back. Single endpoint, client controls the shape.

sections.title: REST vs GraphQL Tradeoffs
content: REST: multiple endpoints, fixed response shape, HTTP caching works naturally
GraphQL: single /graphql endpoint, flexible response, HTTP caching is harder
GraphQL advantage: eliminates over-fetching and under-fetching
GraphQL disadvantage: N+1 query problem if not using DataLoader
GraphQL disadvantage: complex error handling, harder to debug
Spring Boot: Spring for GraphQL (spring-graphql) since Spring Boot 2.7
Use GraphQL: complex clients with many data requirements (mobile apps, dashboards)

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: GraphQL solves a real REST problem: over-fetching and under-fetching. With REST, if I need only a user's name and email, I still get all 20 fields. If I need related data, I make multiple requests. GraphQL sends one request specifying exactly what you need. The tradeoffs: HTTP caching doesn't work as cleanly because all requests go to one endpoint. There's a risk of the N+1 problem where each list item triggers a separate database query — solved with DataLoader. For a standard CRUD backend, REST is simpler. For complex data requirements with many client types, GraphQL shines.

question: What is gRPC and when would you use it instead of REST?
title: gRPC vs REST
direct_answer: gRPC is a high-performance RPC framework using Protocol Buffers (binary format) over HTTP/2. It's faster than REST/JSON for inter-service communication. Use gRPC for internal microservice communication; use REST for public APIs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of the API landscape beyond REST
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying gRPC is better in all cases — it's not suitable for browser clients
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that gRPC uses HTTP/2 and supports streaming

sections.title: gRPC Overview
sections.content: gRPC was created by Google. It uses Protocol Buffers (protobuf) — a binary serialization format that's more compact than JSON. Running over HTTP/2 means multiplexed connections, header compression, and bidirectional streaming. These properties make gRPC ideal for microservice-to-microservice calls where performance matters.

sections.title: gRPC vs REST
content: gRPC: binary protocol (protobuf), REST: text (JSON/XML)
gRPC: HTTP/2, REST: typically HTTP/1.1
gRPC: 5-10x faster serialization than JSON
gRPC: strongly typed via .proto schema files
gRPC: browser support limited (needs grpc-web proxy)
REST: universal browser support, human readable, easier debugging
Use gRPC: internal microservices, high-throughput systems
Use REST: public APIs, browser clients, simple CRUD

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: gRPC uses Protocol Buffers — binary format — over HTTP/2, making it significantly faster than REST with JSON. It also supports streaming and is strongly typed. The downside is that browsers can't use gRPC directly without a proxy. So my rule of thumb: use REST for public-facing APIs and anything a browser or mobile client calls. Use gRPC for internal microservice communication where performance is critical and human readability doesn't matter. At my level, REST is what I'll work with day-to-day, but knowing gRPC exists for performance-sensitive internal communication is valuable.

question: What is the difference between REST and RPC (Remote Procedure Call)?
title: REST vs RPC
direct_answer: REST focuses on resources and uses HTTP verbs to operate on them (GET /users). RPC focuses on actions — you call remote functions (getUser(), createOrder()). REST is noun-centric, RPC is verb-centric.

interviewer_intent.testing: Conceptual understanding of different API styles
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that many 'REST' APIs are actually more RPC-style
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Recognize that REST's resource model is often violated in practice

sections.title: Resource vs Action Oriented
sections.content: REST models the world as resources (nouns): /users, /orders, /products. You act on them with HTTP verbs. RPC models the world as functions (verbs): createUser(), getOrderById(), cancelPayment(). Both can be built over HTTP, but the mental model differs.

sections.title: Key Differences
content: REST: resource-centric, uses HTTP methods as verbs
RPC: action-centric, method name is in the URL or body
REST example: POST /orders creates an order
RPC example: POST /createOrder {orderId: 1, ...}
Many real-world 'REST' APIs are hybrid or RPC-style (POST /users/activate)
JSON-RPC: structured RPC protocol over HTTP
REST is often better for CRUD; RPC is often better for complex workflows

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: The core difference is nouns versus verbs. REST thinks in resources — you have /orders and you GET, POST, PUT, DELETE them. RPC thinks in functions — you call createOrder(), cancelOrder(), getOrderStatus(). Both work over HTTP. In practice, many APIs are hybrid — they're REST for CRUD but RPC-style for complex operations. For example, POST /orders/123/cancel is technically REST-ish but the 'cancel' is a verb action. Pure REST would use PATCH /orders/123 with {status: 'cancelled'}. Recognizing this distinction matters because it affects API predictability.

question: How do you choose between REST, GraphQL, gRPC, and WebSocket for your API?
title: Choosing the Right API Technology
direct_answer: Choose REST for standard CRUD and public APIs. Use GraphQL for complex data requirements with multiple clients needing different shapes. Use gRPC for high-performance internal microservice communication. Use WebSocket for real-time bidirectional communication (chat, live notifications).

interviewer_intent.testing: System design thinking and awareness of technology tradeoffs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Defaulting to REST for everything without considering alternatives
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Frame the decision in terms of the access pattern, client type, and performance requirements

sections.title: API Technology Decision Framework
sections.content: The right API technology depends on who is consuming the API, what the communication pattern is, and what the performance requirements are. There's no single best answer — each technology solves a different problem.

sections.title: Decision Guide
content: REST: public API, browser clients, mobile apps, CRUD operations — default choice
GraphQL: multiple clients (web/mobile) with different data needs, avoids over/under-fetching
gRPC: internal microservice to microservice, high throughput, streaming required
WebSocket: real-time bidirectional — chat apps, live dashboards, collaborative tools
SSE (Server-Sent Events): server pushes updates to browser — simpler than WebSocket for one-way
Webhook: server notifies external system of events (payment callbacks, GitHub webhooks)

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: My decision framework: if it's a public API or browser-facing, REST with JSON is the default — universal support, easy debugging. If different clients need radically different data shapes, GraphQL reduces payload size. For internal microservice calls where performance matters, gRPC's binary protocol and HTTP/2 give significant gains. For real-time features like live notifications or chat, WebSocket enables true bidirectional communication. As a fresher, I'll mostly work with REST, but knowing when each applies shows system design awareness.
